 What to know during this year's Medicare open enrollment period 
 Madalyn Edwards
madalyn.edwards@mtairynews.com

 24 mins ago

 With the Medicare Open Enrollment Period underway, local resources are available for Surry County beneficiaries looking to enroll or change plans.
 “What worked for you this year may not be the best plan for you in 2027,” North Carolina Insurance Commissioner Mike Causey wrote in a statement released this week.
 The traditional open enrollment period began last week on Oct. 15 and will last eight weeks. Any Medicare beneficiary wishing to change his or her traditional plan outside of a qualifying event will need to do so by Dec. 7 to prevent lapse of coverage on Jan. 1.
 Carmen Long, an area extension agent with the North Carolina Cooperative Extension, said even Medicare beneficiaries who are satisfied with their plan should investigate their options during the open enrollment period.
 Some things that may warrant change in Medicare plans include a change of medication, a plan with a formulary that their medication isn’t covered by, and changes from the beneficiary’s provider, to name a few, Long said.
 For provider-related changes, Long encourages people to check with providers to make sure they are in-network, as providers contract different plans each year and don’t always sign up for the same Medicare Advantage plans.
 Review plan each year
 Reviewing plans during open enrollment remains especially significant for Medicare Advantage plans, Long said.
 “Even if you like the plan that you have for this year, just check for the next year, because most people who have a Medicare Advantage plan also get their drug coverage through that Medicare Advantage plan, so we want to make sure that we’re getting the best deal on your medicines as well,” she said.
 For Medicare Advantage plans, there’s a second open-enrollment period which can be used in case a beneficiary’s plan is not working out for them in the new year. The second open enrollment period spans from the beginning of January through the end of March.
 Another significant change from year to year is the price of plans, Long said.
 “We just want to make sure that the person’s medicines are covered and if they can be covered on a less expensive plan,” she said. “There’s no need to pay a really high premium for a plan that might not really save them any money.”
 A new maximum deductible for prescription drug coverage has moved up to $700, but Long said she doesn’t want the price increase to intimidate people.
 “A lot of times, if people are taking generic medications, they really don’t have to meet that deductible,” she said.
 Deciding on coverage during a qualifying event and even open-enrollment can be stressful, said Long, so she often employs a helpful analogy to describe important considerations.
 When visiting three different stores and buying the same box of cereal at each, both price and customer service will vary at each store. Long said the same mentality applies to Medicare plans, particularly for Medicare supplemental plans and Medicare Advantage, which are provided through different companies. Even with the same coverage and services, the same two factors will vary, so it’s important to investigate the best option for each beneficiary.
 And even if beneficiaries are satisfied with price and customer service, Long still encourages them to review their coverage during open enrollment, as she said she’s heard of cases where providers have moved customers to a different plan if the current plan has ended.
 Help available
 Long said volunteers working in the Senior Health Insurance Information Program, or SHIIP, can help people figure out which plan covers their medication for the least amount of money, and can also look at the difference in cost of medications with their drug plan at different pharmacies. Sometimes, she explained, switching pharmacies can save people money because different pharmacies work closely with those drug prescription plans.
 Three volunteers are working for SHIIP in Surry County, and Long said they are always looking for more experienced volunteers willing to take online training to meet one-on-one with clients to discuss all the options that are available to them.
 SHIIP counseling is free and can be conducted by appointment over the phone or in-person at offices in either the North Carolina Cooperative Extension building in Dobson or the Human Services Building in Mount Airy. Those wishing to schedule an appointment or inquire about services can do so by calling 336-401-8025.
 North Carolina has 11 stand-alone prescription drug plans to choose from, which are available in every county, and range from as low as $5.30 to $239.20 a month. Everyone should sign up for a plan when they first become eligible for Medicare, Long said, even if they don’t take medications. Those who do not sign up when they turn 65 will carry a penalty that is automatically added to their premiums that doesn’t go away.
 “We encourage people to just pick a very cheap or inexpensive plan, and that way, if they find out they’re going to need a medication, it’ll also keep them from having that penalty,” she said.
 For Medicare Advantage plans in Surry County, there are 31 available plans that are zip code specific. Long said just because a TV advertisement claims a plan will ensure beneficiaries receive benefits for free doesn’t mean it’s available in Surry County.
 When considering the differences between Advantage plans and stand-along Medicare plans with a Medicare prescription drug plan, there are advantages and disadvantages both ways, Long advised.
 For Medicare Advantage, plans provide some vision, hearing and dental coverage alongside some over-the-counter benefits, but beneficiaries must use in-network providers and it typically require co-pays for most services.
 “So, it doesn’t provide the flexibility that a traditional Medicare plan provides,” she said.
 Alternatively, a traditional Medicare and a Medicare supplemental policy can help pick up what Medicare doesn’t cover, but often has higher premiums up front compared to an Advantage plan.
 “They are both good, they’re both helpful, they’re just different. And for some people, they feel more comfortable paying that higher premium and having the peace of mind that they can go to any doctor they need to go to, and that works well for them,” Long said. “Other people who don’t want to spend as much on a monthly basis for that premium may feel like they do better with those Medicare Advantage plans.”
 For both traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage, one thing that remains true for both is that they both offer preventative benefits. Long encourages beneficiaries to take a list of preventative benefits with them during provider visits to inquire about them.
 “We know that if the issues are found in the early stages, it’s easier for the patient, and it saves a lot of money in the long run,” she said.
 Looping in family members for Medicare-related decisions or asking them for help is also advisable, according to Long, as well as consulting with a trusted insurance agent. Long said her department appreciates the work of insurance agents with open-enrollment decisions, but emphasized that the Department of Insurance doesn’t make money from helping and consulting people through SHIIP, so they are able to provide a non-biased perspective when counseling.
 Long’s department also works on educating beneficiaries on Medicare fraud and abuse through SHIIP, and she always encourages beneficiaries to read their Medicare summary notices to ensure they were billed correctly. Incorrect billing of services can be expensive and lead to access issues to those services if the bill incorrectly indicates they’ve already been done, she said.
 “All the information that is entered in is subject to human error, so sometimes things happen by mistake,” Long said, “and sometimes things happen whenever people try to scam someone. So it is important that we pay attention to that.”
 Free shredding event
 To improve Medicare-related security initiatives through the open-enrollment period, the department will host a free shredding event on Nov. 14 at Pilot Mountain First United Methodist Church.
 Long said right now is a good time to get together sensitive documents that contain Medicare numbers, health insurance information or anything other documents containing identity-related information to prioritize safety and reduce scams and fraud.
 In addition to taking advantage of local SHIIP services, the statement from the North Carolina Department of Health Insurance also encouraged beneficiaries to take action by reviewing the Medicare & You handbook mailed to Medicare recipients in September, visiting the medicare website to review options and make changes and calling the 24/7 Medicare hotline at 1-800-MEDICARE to learn more about coverage.
